title: 1 Chronicles 29:20–30
context: David calls the assembly to bless the LORD; they worship, offer abundant sacrifices, and make Solomon king a second time, anointing him as prince and Zadok as priest. Solomon sits on the throne of the LORD, all Israel and David’s sons submit to him, and the LORD magnifies him; the book closes with David’s forty-year reign, his death at a good old age, and the histories of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad. The Chronicler’s succession scene is quieter than the account in 1 Kings 1–2, and both traditions read each on its own terms without harmonizing them.

verses.text: Then David said to all the assembly, “Now bless the LORD your God!” All the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed down their heads and prostrated themselves before the LORD and the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now bless the LORD your God!” The assembly blesses the LORD and bows down “before the LORD and the king.” Arminian readers note that the people’s worship responds to David’s call.

Honor to the king is set within worship of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the assembly joining David’s prayer with their own praise.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the bowing before the king expresses respect for God’s appointed ruler, not worship of the king himself.

verses.text: They sacrificed sacrifices to the LORD and offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the next day after that day, even one thousand bulls, one thousand rams, and one thousand lambs, with their drink offerings and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel,
verses.arminianNotes:
They offer a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, “with their drink offerings and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel.” Arminian readers note the scale of the celebration.

The offerings express thanksgiving for God’s provision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the sacrifices as worship and communal celebration.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the joy of the occasion is expressed in offerings shared “for all Israel.”

verses.text: and ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. They made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and anointed him before the LORD to be prince, and Zadok to be priest.
verses.arminianNotes:
They “ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness” and “made Solomon the son of David king the second time.” Arminian readers note that the first notice is in 23:1.

1 Kings 1 describes Solomon’s anointing at Gihon amid Adonijah’s bid for the throne; the accounts are read side by side.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note that Zadok is anointed “to be priest” (cf. 1 Kings 2:35).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both leave the relation between this public confirmation and the account in 1 Kings 1 without harmonizing.

verses.text: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king instead of David his father, and prospered; and all Israel obeyed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king instead of David his father, and prospered; and all Israel obeyed him.” Arminian readers note the phrase “the throne of the LORD,” which presents the king as ruling under God.

1 Kings 2:12 also records Solomon sitting on his father’s throne.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s choice of Solomon (28:5) now realized.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the kingdom belongs to the LORD, and Solomon reigns as his appointed king.

verses.text: All the princes, the mighty men, and also all of the sons of King David submitted themselves to Solomon the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the princes, the mighty men, and also all of the sons of King David submitted themselves to Solomon the king.” Arminian readers note the Chronicler’s emphasis on unity.

1 Kings 1–2 records Adonijah’s bid for the throne; the Chronicler does not mention it, and the accounts are not harmonized here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the Chronicler’s focus on Israel’s united support for Solomon.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the two books give different emphases, and each is read on its own terms.

verses.text: The LORD magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and gave to him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and gave to him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.” Arminian readers note that Solomon’s honor is God’s gift.

The verse anticipates 1 Kings 3:13.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God as the one who exalts.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: royal majesty is received from the LORD, which echoes David’s confession in 29:12.

verses.text: Now David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.” Arminian readers note the summary that begins the close of David’s reign.

The phrase “son of Jesse” recalls his humble beginnings (cf. 2 Sam 23:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the summary of a reign established by God’s choice (28:4).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler presents David as king over all Israel, a theme throughout the book.

verses.text: The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years; he reigned seven years in Hebron, and he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years; he reigned seven years in Hebron, and he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the figures match 1 Kings 2:11.

2 Samuel 5:5 gives a more precise figure for Hebron.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the numbers stand as given.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the reign is counted and closed, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 2:11.

verses.text: He died at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor; and Solomon his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He died at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor; and Solomon his son reigned in his place.” Arminian readers note the peaceful summary of David’s death, which recalls Abraham (Gen 25:8).

The Chronicler’s account is brief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of God’s blessing on David.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler’s quieter account stands beside 1 Kings 1–2 without being harmonized.

verses.text: Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Samuel the seer, and in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the history of Gad the seer,
verses.arminianNotes:
David’s acts “are written in the history of Samuel the seer, and in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the history of Gad the seer.” Arminian readers note the prophetic sources cited.

The relation of these works to the books we have is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prophetic witness to David’s reign.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler points readers to the prophets who spoke into David’s life.

verses.text: with all his reign and his might, and the events that involved him, Israel, and all the kingdoms of the lands.
verses.arminianNotes:
The record includes “all his reign and his might, and the events that involved him, Israel, and all the kingdoms of the lands.” Arminian readers note that the book closes by pointing to a fuller record.

The Chronicler selects what serves his purpose.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s reign set within God’s dealings with Israel and the nations.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the book ends with David’s reign complete and the throne passed to Solomon.
